transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I suppose I’m here because I’ve been feeling like something in me has sort of settled into this discouraging place. Not in a dramatic way, exactly. It’s more quiet than that, but it’s stubborn. I keep having this feeling that the best version of my life is behind me, and that no matter how much I try to plan things out or be disciplined or tell myself to get on with it, I don’t really get back to feeling like myself.

I’m 65, so I know some of that sounds like ordinary aging, and I don’t want to make too much of it. But it feels deeper than just getting older. It’s like I’ve lost confidence that effort will actually change much. That’s what finally made me think I should come in and talk to someone.
Can you describe how your mood has been lately? Specifically, do you find that you feel down or discouraged most days, and does that feeling last throughout the day?

Yes… most days, I’d say. It’s not that I’m crying all the time or unable to speak to people or anything like that. From the outside I probably look fairly normal, maybe just quieter. But there’s this low, gray tone underneath things almost all the time.

Even when I’m doing something I used to associate with feeling absorbed, like being in the studio, it’s still there in the background. Or I’ll be sitting across from my wife at dinner, and nothing bad is happening, we’re just having a perfectly ordinary evening, and I can still feel it sitting there. Discouragement is probably the best word. Not dramatic despair, more like a dull heaviness that colors the day. It tends to stretch through most of the day, yes, though some moments are easier to ignore than others.
Have you noticed that you take less pleasure or interest in activities that you used to enjoy, like being in the studio or spending time with your wife?

I’m not completely sure how to answer that, because it’s not as simple as “I don’t enjoy anything anymore.” I wouldn’t want to overstate it. There are still moments where I can appreciate things, or at least recognize that they matter to me.

With the studio, for example, I still go in there, and sometimes I can get caught up in the process a little. But there’s also this… distance from it, I suppose. Like I know it used to mean something more immediate to me, and now I’m often just going through the motions until I eventually settle into it, if I do at all.

And with my wife, I care about her very much. I don’t want to give the impression that I don’t enjoy being with her. But sometimes even when we’re together and it should feel easy, I’m aware of myself not quite being present in the way I’d like to be. So yes and no, I guess. I haven’t lost all interest, but things don’t seem to reach me as readily as they used to.
Can you describe your mood first thing in the morning, before anything has really happened in the day? Does it feel low or heavy right away, or does it tend to settle in later?

In the morning… yes, I think it’s often there pretty early. Not always in some sharp, obvious way, like waking up and thinking, “Oh, today is terrible.” It’s quieter than that. But before anything has really happened, before I’ve even had a chance to be disappointed by the day, there can already be this sort of gray cast over things.

I’ll wake up and lie there for a bit, and it’s not that I’m in tears or overwhelmed. It’s more that the day already feels a little heavy, like I’m starting from underneath something. Then I get up and do what I’m supposed to do, and sometimes the routine distracts me. If I go into the studio, or I’m having breakfast with my wife, I can function and even seem normal enough. But that low tone is usually still running underneath it.

So I wouldn’t say it only settles in later. It may become more noticeable as the day goes on, depending on what I’m doing, but most days it’s there from the beginning in some form.
Can you say more about whether you’ve noticed a change in how you feel pleasure or interest, even in things you used to care about?

I’m not sure I can pin it down more neatly than what I was saying before. I do notice something different, yes, but it’s hard for me to separate “less pleasure” from just feeling generally dulled out.

Like, I still care about the things I’ve always cared about. I don’t feel as if I’ve suddenly become a different person with different values. If I’m in the studio, I know it matters to me, and there are still moments where I can look at something I’m working on and think, “All right, that’s not nothing.” But the feeling doesn’t come as quickly, or as warmly, maybe. It’s more effortful. I have to sort of work my way into caring, instead of it being there naturally.

And with my wife, it’s similar. I want to be present with her, and I do still enjoy being with her in a quieter way. But sometimes I’m aware that I’m responding from a little distance, if that makes sense. Like I know I should be feeling more than I am in the moment, or I remember that I used to feel it more immediately.

So I wouldn’t say pleasure is gone. That sounds too absolute. It’s more muted. Things still matter, but they don’t always reach me the way they used to.
Can you recall if there have been any recent events that you would consider positive or uplifting, and if so, did your mood improve at all during or after those events?

Yes, there have been a few things I’d call positive, or at least things that by any reasonable standard should feel positive. I mean, nothing spectacular, but small things — a decent stretch in the studio where something starts to come together, or a quiet dinner with my wife where the conversation is pleasant and there isn’t any tension. Those are good moments. I can recognize them as good.

But the way my mood responds is… limited, I suppose. It may lift a little while I’m in it, especially if I’m absorbed enough not to be watching myself so closely. But most days I’m not in tears or anything dramatic; there’s just this low, gray tone running underneath everything. Even when I’m in the studio, or sitting across from my wife at dinner, it’s still there in the background.

So I wouldn’t say positive things do nothing. That wouldn’t be fair. They can soften it a bit, maybe give me a short break from paying attention to it. But it doesn’t feel like they clear it away. It’s more like the surface changes for a while, and underneath that the same heaviness is still running.

Can you describe if, and how often, you experience a sense of enjoyment or satisfaction when engaging in activities you used to find meaningful, like being in the studio or spending time with your wife?

I’m not sure I can give you a clean frequency, like “three times a week” or something. It doesn’t really present itself that neatly to me.

With the studio, there are still times when I get some satisfaction, yes. If I’ve been struggling with something and then one part of it starts to make sense, I can feel a kind of quiet approval, or relief maybe. But I don’t always know if I’d call it enjoyment in the fuller sense. Sometimes I’m there doing the work because it’s what I do, and because I still believe it matters, but the feeling of being carried along by it doesn’t always show up.

And with my wife, I do have moments that feel good — sitting together, talking, even just being in the same room in a peaceful way. I don’t want to make it sound like I feel nothing, because that wouldn’t be true. But the enjoyment is often softer, more muted. It’s not absent, exactly, but it can feel like I’m receiving it from a little farther away than I used to.

As for how often… I suppose it happens intermittently. There are moments of satisfaction or warmth, but they don’t always last, and they don’t always shift the whole mood of the day. It’s more like small patches of light rather than the general atmosphere changing.
Have you found that you’ve lost interest or pleasure in most activities, even those that used to matter a lot to you, not just some of the time, but most of the time?

I’m not sure I’d put it that strongly. “Most activities, most of the time” sounds a little too broad, or too final, compared with how it feels from inside.

I don’t think I’ve lost interest in everything, or even in most things in a clean way. It’s more that the interest is harder to access. The things that matter still matter — I don’t feel indifferent to them, exactly. But I can go through stretches where I’m doing them more out of commitment or habit than because there’s a real pull toward them.

So if you’re asking whether pleasure is gone most of the time, I’d say no, not gone. Muted, yes. Inconsistent. Sometimes I have to get started before I feel anything at all, and sometimes even then it stays fairly flat. But I wouldn’t want to exaggerate it and say I’ve lost interest in most activities altogether. It’s more like the volume has been turned down, and I notice that a lot.
Can you describe how your mood is later in the day, especially when there’s not much going on? Does the low feeling tend to stay with you even when things are calm or routine?

Yes… it does tend to stay with me. Later in the day, especially if there isn’t much happening, I notice it more, I think. Not because it suddenly becomes dramatic, exactly — I’m not usually falling apart or crying or anything like that. It’s more that when the day gets quieter, there’s less to cover it over.

It’s this low, gray sort of feeling that sits underneath things. I can be doing something ordinary, making dinner, sitting in the house, even having a perfectly calm evening with my wife, and it’s still there in the background. Sometimes if I’m absorbed in the studio or in conversation, I can forget it for a while, or it feels less prominent. But once things settle down, it’s as if I become aware of the same heaviness again.

So yes, calm or routine doesn’t necessarily make it go away. In some ways the quiet makes it easier to hear, if that makes sense. It’s not a sharp sadness most of the time. It’s more like the whole day has a muted color to it, and even when nothing is wrong in the moment, that tone is still running underneath.

Would you say that your mood stays pretty much the same throughout the day, with only small shifts even when things are going well, or do you have more noticeable ups and downs depending on what’s happening?

I’d say it’s mostly steady, unfortunately. There are shifts, but they’re not usually big dramatic swings where I feel fine in the morning and terrible by evening, or the other way around. It’s more like… the baseline is low, and then things can brighten it a little or dull it a little, depending on what’s happening.

Most days I’m not in tears or anything dramatic like that. I can still function, I can talk, I can be in the studio, I can sit across from my wife at dinner and have a perfectly ordinary conversation. But underneath all of that there’s this low, gray tone that seems to keep running. Even when something is going well, it doesn’t always lift the whole thing. It might give me a small bit of relief or warmth, but the basic mood doesn’t completely change.

So I suppose I do have ups and downs, but they’re small ones, within a pretty narrow range. The day may get a little lighter if I’m absorbed in something, or if there’s a good moment with my wife, but it’s not as though the heaviness disappears. It’s more like it recedes a bit and then comes back into view when things quiet down.
Would you say that your low mood is present most of the day, nearly every day, even if it's not always intense or dramatic?

Yes, I think that’s fair. It’s present most of the day, most days, though I’d qualify it by saying it isn’t usually dramatic. I’m not walking around sobbing, and I’m not unable to speak or function or anything like that.

It’s more like this low, gray tone running underneath everything. Even when I’m in the studio, or sitting across from my wife at dinner, or doing something ordinary that should feel neutral or even pleasant, there’s still that background heaviness. Sometimes I’m distracted enough that I don’t notice it as much, but when I check in with myself, it’s usually there.

So yes — not always intense, but pretty constant. It colors the day more often than not.
Would you say that your low mood has been present nearly every day for most of the day, even if it varies in intensity?

Yes… yes, I would say that. I know I’ve probably said it a few different ways, but that really is how it feels. Most days I’m not in tears or anything dramatic like that, and I can still go through the day in a fairly ordinary way. But there’s this low, gray tone underneath everything.

It can be there even when I’m in the studio, or when I’m just sitting across from my wife at dinner and nothing especially bad is happening. It may fade into the background if I’m occupied, but it doesn’t really leave. It varies a bit, sure — some moments are lighter than others — but most of the day, nearly every day, there’s that same heaviness running underneath.
Would you say that you’ve lost interest or pleasure in nearly all of your activities, even the ones that used to matter a lot to you?

I’m not sure I’d put it that strongly. “Nearly all” feels a bit too broad for what I experience.

There are things that don’t give me as much as they used to, yes, or that feel muted. I can still do them, and sometimes I can even get absorbed in them for a while, but the pleasure isn’t always very vivid. It’s more subdued, like the volume has been turned down.

But I wouldn’t say I’ve lost interest in everything, or that nothing matters to me anymore. Some things still do matter. They just don’t always lift me in the way I think they once did, or in the way I’d expect them to. So… no, not a complete loss of interest or pleasure across nearly everything. More a dulling, I suppose.
Would you say that activities you used to enjoy, like being in the studio or spending time with your wife, feel flat or empty most of the time, even when you’re doing them?

I’d say… yes, in the sense that even when I’m doing those things, there’s still this flatness underneath. I don’t know if I’d call it completely empty, because that sounds a little more absolute than it feels, but there is definitely a kind of dullness to it.

When I’m in the studio, for example, I can still go through the motions, and sometimes I’m paying attention to what I’m doing. But it’s as if there’s a gray film over it. It doesn’t quite reach me the way I expect it to. And with my wife, even just sitting at dinner, nothing bad happening, I can be there and participate and talk, but that low mood is still running in the background.

Most days I’m not crying or visibly falling apart. It’s not dramatic like that. It’s more that steady, low, gray tone underneath things, even during moments that should feel meaningful or comforting. So yes, a lot of the time those activities don’t feel as full as they used to.
Would you say that you experience little to no pleasure or interest in almost all of your usual activities, even ones you used to enjoy a lot?

I don’t think I can quite say “little to no” pleasure or interest in almost everything. That sounds too total, if that makes sense.

It’s more complicated than that for me. I do still care about some of my usual activities, and I can still get something from them at times. Being in the studio, for instance — it doesn’t always feel alive or satisfying in the way I want it to, and sometimes I’m just sort of doing it because it’s what I do. But I wouldn’t say there’s no interest there. It’s still part of me.

And with my wife, too, I don’t feel empty toward her or uninterested in being with her. It’s just that the enjoyment feels dulled sometimes, like I’m present but not fully warmed by it. So I suppose I’d say the pleasure is muted, not absent. I wouldn’t say almost all of my activities have no pleasure or meaning. It’s more that even when there is some, it often doesn’t come through very strongly.
Would you say that you experience little to no pleasure or interest in almost all of your usual activities, even ones you used to enjoy a lot?

I think I’m probably circling the same answer, but no, I wouldn’t quite say “little to no” pleasure or interest in almost all of them. That feels like a stronger statement than I can honestly make.

It’s more that things feel… reduced. Blunted, maybe. I can still care about certain things, and I can still have moments where I’m engaged, or at least interested enough to keep going. But the enjoyment doesn’t always rise up very clearly. It’s not the same as feeling nothing at all.

So if you’re asking whether almost everything I normally do feels completely pointless or pleasureless, I don’t think that’s right. But if you’re asking whether the pleasure is often quieter than it used to be, or harder to access, then yes, that’s closer. It’s just not absent across the board.
Would you say that you’ve experienced a clear loss of interest or pleasure in almost everything you do, to the point where even things you used to really care about feel meaningless or unimportant?

I’m not sure I’d put it that strongly, no. “Almost everything” and “meaningless” feel a little too far for what I experience.

There are definitely times when things feel dulled down, like I’ve said — like the color has gone out of them somewhat. But I don’t feel as if the things I care about have become unimportant to me. I still know they matter. I still care about being in the studio, and I still care very much about my wife. It’s more that the feeling of enjoyment doesn’t always come with the same force, or it takes longer to show up, or sometimes it’s just quieter than I think it should be.

So… no, I wouldn’t say there’s a clear loss of interest or pleasure in almost everything to the point that it all feels meaningless. It’s more like a muted pleasure, or a distance from it, rather than everything becoming empty or irrelevant.
Would you say that you have experienced a loss of interest or pleasure in almost all of your activities most of the day, nearly every day, even in things you used to really enjoy?

I don’t think I can say that, no — not in that “almost all activities, most of the day, nearly every day” kind of way.

I mean, I do notice that enjoyment can feel muted or slow to arrive, and sometimes I’ll be doing something I used to really enjoy and I’ll think, “Why doesn’t this feel like it should?” But that’s different from feeling like I’ve lost interest in nearly everything all day long. There are still things I care about. There are still moments where I’m engaged, even if they’re not as bright or as effortless as I’d like.

So… I’d say no, not a loss of interest or pleasure in almost everything, nearly every day. More like the pleasure is inconsistent or dulled at times, but not gone.
Would you say that you have experienced a loss of interest or pleasure in almost all of your activities most of the day, nearly every day, even in things you used to really enjoy?

I realize I’m repeating myself a bit, but no, I don’t think I can say that in the full way you’re asking it — not “almost all activities,” and not “most of the day, nearly every day.”

It’s more uneven than that for me. Some things can feel flatter than I’d like, and sometimes I notice that the enjoyment doesn’t come as naturally as it used to. But I wouldn’t say I’ve lost interest in nearly everything, or that even the things I used to enjoy have become empty to me. That doesn’t feel accurate.

So if you’re asking very specifically whether it’s a near-constant loss of pleasure across almost everything, I’d have to say no. It’s more muted at times than gone.
